h1: Planning mixed fermentation sour beer timelines in tropical heat
title: Mixed fermentation sours in the heat | Craft Beer School
desc: How heat changes the timeline of mixed fermentation sour beer in India, what to control and how to plan from brew day to bottling.
teaser: Mixed fermentation sours often take a year in a cool cellar. In Indian heat the clock runs faster. So do the risks.
standfirst: Brettanomyces, lactic bacteria and brewer's yeast work together in a mixed fermentation. Heat changes how fast each one acts. We explain how to plan timelines, control risk and know when a sour beer is ready.
sections:
A mixed fermentation sour beer uses several microbes together, usually brewer's yeast, Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus and Pediococcus. Each contributes something different: alcohol, acidity, funk and complexity.

Unlike a kettle sour, which is soured quickly before boiling, a mixed fermentation develops slowly. In temperate climates, many traditional sours take six months to well over a year before they are ready. Our guide to Brettanomyces covers the yeast that drives much of that slow change.
What heat does to the microbes

Most microbes work faster when it is warmer, up to a point. In a typical Indian summer, ambient temperatures in an unconditioned room can run well above 30 °C. That has several effects:

  • Saccharomyces finishes primary fermentation quickly, with more esters and higher alcohols.
  • Lactobacillus produces acid faster.
  • Brettanomyces works faster, breaking down sugars that brewer's yeast left behind.
  • Pediococcus can produce diacetyl and ropiness, which Brett then needs time to clean up.

The timeline shortens, but control becomes harder.

Higher temperatures bring specific risks:

  • Acetic acid. Acetobacter turns alcohol into vinegar when oxygen is present. Warm conditions speed it up.
  • Harsh fusel alcohols. From a hot primary fermentation.
  • Mousiness. A defect linked to some Brett and lactic bacteria, often described as tasting like a mouse cage. It is hard to pick up by smell and usually shows as an aftertaste.
  • Over-acidification. Sourness can outrun the other flavours before Brett develops.

Our guide to fermenting through an Indian summer covers heat control for all beers.

Mixed fermentations do not need cold temperatures, but they do need stable ones. Many brewers aim for a steady range around 18 to 22 °C, which allows good activity without runaway fermentation.

Options include:

  • Ferment primary in a glycol-jacketed fermenter, then move to a temperature-controlled room for ageing.
  • Insulate and air condition a small barrel or tank room.
  • Avoid placing ageing vessels near walls that get direct sun.

One brewhouse-floor detail: wooden barrels in warm rooms lose liquid through evaporation faster and can let in more oxygen. Top them up regularly with the same beer. Check for leaks after hot spells.
A sample timeline in controlled conditions

With temperature control, a typical plan might look like this:

  1. Week 1 to 2. Primary fermentation with Saccharomyces, often with lactic bacteria pitched alongside or soon after.
  2. Month 1 to 3. Brett and bacteria work on remaining sugars. Acidity climbs.
  3. Month 3 to 6. Flavour develops. Taste monthly, track gravity and pH.
  4. Month 6 onwards. Blend or package once gravity is stable for several weeks and flavour is balanced.

This is an example, not a rule. Each strain, wort and vessel behaves differently. The only reliable test is stable gravity over time and a flavour you are happy with.

Never package a mixed fermentation sour on a calendar date. Brett can keep fermenting sugars and dextrins slowly for months. If you bottle too early, pressure builds and bottles can burst.

Check gravity over several weeks. If it has not changed, the beer is likely stable. Measure pH and titratable acidity to track sourness. Taste for diacetyl, acetic notes and mousiness. Our guide to kettle souring describes a faster, more predictable alternative if you need sours on a short schedule.

A mixed fermentation programme lives on its records. For every vessel, log the brew date, wort gravity, microbes pitched, temperature, gravity and pH at each check and tasting notes. Without them, a good barrel cannot be repeated and a bad one cannot be explained.

Records also show how heat changes your timeline. After a year of logs, you will know how much faster your summer batches move than your winter ones, which is better than any rule of thumb from a cooler country.

Brett and lactic bacteria are hard to remove from soft materials such as gaskets, hoses and plastic. Many breweries keep separate equipment for sour beers, including transfer hoses, gaskets, fittings and bottling equipment. Clean and sanitise thoroughly. Label everything.

A single cross-contamination can sour a whole tank of clean lager. In a busy brewpub, that is a costly mistake.

Planning a sour programme in Indian conditions takes more than one recipe. It needs strain choice, temperature control and a clear plan for blending and packaging. That is where structured training saves time and dumped beer.
faqs: How long does a mixed fermentation sour take in India?
With temperature control, many are ready in six months or more. Heat speeds things up but adds risk, so judge readiness by stable gravity and flavour, not the calendar.
What temperature should I age sour beer at?
Many brewers aim for a stable range around 18 to 22 °C. Avoid big swings and direct sun on ageing vessels.
Why do sour beer bottles sometimes explode?
Brett can keep fermenting slowly. Packaging before gravity is stable lets pressure build in the bottle.
